{"result":"# The Rust Programming Language and Memory Safety

Rust balances performance, type safety, concurrency, and memory safety in a general-purpose language [1]. Graydon Hoare began developing it in 2006, and Mozilla Research later sponsored and maintained it starting in 2009 [2].

Memory safety protects programs from bugs and security vulnerabilities in memory access, such as buffer overflows and dangling pointers [3]. Java is memory-safe because its runtime checks array bounds and pointer dereferences [3]. By contrast, C, C++, and Fortran permit arbitrary pointer arithmetic without bounds checking, making them memory-unsafe [3].

Rust resembles C++ in syntax but guarantees memory safety without a garbage collector [2]. It also replaces classes and inheritance with structs, enums, traits, and methods [1]. Functional influences such as immutability, algebraic data types, and pattern matching shape how programmers structure their code [1].

Memory safety remains central to modern systems software, and Rust shows that strong guarantees and low-level control can coexist.
